title: Discover what's next for AI, from the SaaS reckoning to the agent security gap, at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
author: Modelverse Editorial
excerpt: At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, the AI Stage is back to dig into the single hottest topic in the community for the past few years, presented by Google for Startups.
body:
TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is set to host its dedicated AI Stage from October 13–15 in San Francisco, presented by Google for Startups, to dissect the profound shifts AI has brought across the startup ecosystem. The event will move beyond foundational AI capabilities to explore its disruptive impact on core business functions, including how companies sell, secure data, and scale. Key themes will encompass the redefinition of business models, the emergence of critical security vulnerabilities, and the creation of entirely new job categories driven by AI.

The AI Stage will delve into pressing questions facing founders and the broader AI community. Discussions will tackle the complexities of pricing AI products as models become increasingly commoditized, the urgent need to rebuild agent security from the ground up to address new infrastructure challenges, and what constitutes an effective go-to-market strategy in an AI-native landscape. Experts will also break down the evolving requirements for enterprise AI security in 2026, covering essential aspects like observability, governance, and architectural best practices for trusted deployments. Furthermore, sessions will explore the progression of visual AI from captivating demonstrations to real-time inference and sophisticated physical reasoning.

For developers and researchers, these discussions are paramount. The insights offered will be crucial for navigating the commercialization of AI, understanding the next generation of security challenges in autonomous systems, and identifying new opportunities in fields like GTM engineering, which has rapidly become a high-growth area. By addressing the practicalities of AI deployment, security, and market strategy, the event provides a vital platform for the AI community to understand current demands, anticipate future trends, and contribute to building more robust and impactful AI solutions.

title: Thinking Machines co-founder Lilian Weng left the company citing health reasons, then joined OpenAI
author: Modelverse Editorial
excerpt: Weng previously served as the VP of AI Safety Research at OpenAI.
body:
Lilian Weng, a co-founder of Thinking Machines, recently announced her departure from the startup, citing health concerns stemming from the intense stress and workload inherent in a fast-paced startup environment. This decision, shared publicly, highlighted the personal toll that demanding roles in the tech industry can take. Shortly after this announcement, it was revealed that Weng would be rejoining OpenAI, where she previously held the position of VP of AI Safety Research.

At OpenAI, Weng is set to lead a crucial top-level team dedicated to accelerating the company's internal research initiatives. A key focus for her team will be to support cross-research efforts in recursive self-improvement. This advanced concept involves developing AI systems capable of iteratively enhancing their own capabilities, essentially learning to make themselves more powerful over time. Her role will be pivotal in pushing the boundaries of OpenAI's foundational AI development.

This high-profile talent acquisition is significant for both developers and researchers in the AI community. Weng's move underscores the fierce competition for top-tier expertise among leading AI labs. Her leadership in accelerating research, particularly in recursive self-improvement, signals OpenAI's commitment to exploring cutting-edge methods for AI advancement. For the broader AI landscape, this shift could influence the pace and direction of future AI capabilities, making her contribution to OpenAI's core research trajectory a critical development to watch.

title: Prompt Engineering vs Loop Engineering vs Graph Engineering: What Changes at Each Layer
author: Modelverse Editorial
excerpt: Three terms now compete for the same line in AI engineering job descriptions. Prompt engineering is the established one. Loop engineering entered the AI vocabulary in late 2025 and...
body:
Modelverse highlights a crucial evolution in AI engineering, introducing a hierarchical framework that distinguishes between Prompt, Loop, and Graph Engineering. These aren't competing methodologies but rather stacked units of control, each building upon the last. Prompt engineering, the foundational layer, governs a single model's response. Loop engineering, which emerged in late 2025, elevates this by automating the prompting process within an agent's behavior cycle. The most recent addition, Graph engineering (mid-2026), sits at the apex, orchestrating the organization and interaction of multiple agents.

This progression is vital for developers and researchers as it addresses the limitations of relying solely on prompt engineering for complex AI tasks. The traditional model, requiring human judgment and revision at every iteration, becomes impractical for high-volume, multi-step processes where results must automatically feed into subsequent steps without constant human oversight. The shift towards Loop and Graph engineering enables the creation of more autonomous and sophisticated AI systems, allowing for the design of intricate workflows and collaborative agent architectures that can operate at scale, significantly reducing the need for continuous human intervention.
